title: Tiny Asteroid Becomes Earth's Temporary Minimoon Until Early 2027
site_name: ColombiaOne: News from Colombia and the World
excerpt: Earth has captured asteroid 2026 QQ8, a tiny minimoon discovered in August that is expected to escape Earth's gravity by early 2027.
content:
Earth’s temporary minimoon, a tiny asteroid called 2026 QQ8, measures about six feet (2 meters) across. Astronomers say Earth’s gravity captured it in April 2026 and expect it to escape between late 2026 and early 2027, following observations that established its temporary orbit and natural origin.

Scientists call this kind of visitor a minimoon, a small asteroid that Earth’s gravity captures for a few months or years before the Sun’s gravitational pull draws it away. It does not affect the tides or the night sky and cannot be seen without a large telescope.

The discovery matters less for the rock itself than for what it reveals. Astronomers now believe Earth holds at least one minimoon at any given moment, and the arrival of new telescopes means these hidden companions could soon become easier to detect.

Earth’s temporary minimoon arrived in April but escaped detection until August

2026 QQ8 slipped into Earth’s orbit unnoticed. Hungarian astronomer Krisztian Sarneczky spotted it in August 2026 from the Piszkesteto Observatory in Hungary. Calculations tracing its path backward show that it crossed into Earth’s Hill sphere (the region where Earth’s gravitational influence can dominate the Sun’s) in April, with its closest approach on May 1.

Confirming its origin took more work than finding it. The first question was whether the object was natural or human-made space debris. Follow-up observations with the University of Hawaii 2.2-meter telescope and the Lowell Discovery Telescope in Arizona allowed the Minor Planet Center of the International Astronomical Union to rule out an artificial origin when it published the orbit on Oct. 29.

That orbit explains the rock’s short stay. 2026 QQ8 circles the Sun in 359 days, almost exactly like Earth, and passes our planet about every 10 years at roughly 1.5 times the Moon’s distance. Each visit leaves it just enough time to complete a loop and a half before drifting away.

How minimoons differ from quasi-moons

The word “moon” can be misleading here. A true minimoon stays gravitationally bound to Earth for a period, whereas a quasi-moon, an asteroid that shares Earth’s roughly one-year orbit around the Sun and only appears to circle our planet, is not gravitationally bound to Earth. Astronomers distinguish between the two for that reason.

History shows how rare confirmed cases have been. The asteroid 1991 VG, a rock about 30 feet (10 meters) wide, was discovered in November 1991 and has been discussed as a possible minimoon. Another object, 2024 PT5, followed with a two-month stay in 2024 that some scientists link to debris blasted off our Moon.

Quasi-moons last longer and attract more interest. Kamoʻoalewa, a 40-meter asteroid discovered in 2016, is a prime target for China’s Tianwen-2 mission, which plans to bring back samples in 2027. Meanwhile, 2025 PN7, measuring about 62 to 98 feet (19 to 30 meters) across, is expected to remain near Earth for roughly 60 years. Both objects could help scientists investigate whether such companions originated from the Moon.

New telescopes could reveal more minimoons

Most minimoons remain temporarily captured for less than a year, though some may stay for decades. Their small size and faint light help explain why astronomers have missed nearly all of them until recently. A six-foot rock reflects too little sunlight for most surveys to detect unless it passes very close to Earth.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile could change that. It began operating earlier this year and is designed to scan the Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, allowing it to detect objects moving quickly against the stars. Over its planned 10-year survey, it is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects, potentially including many minimoons entering and leaving Earth’s orbit.

Sources still disagree on some details of 2026 QQ8, with estimates of its width ranging from three to six feet and its departure expected between December and January. However, none indicate that the asteroid poses a danger. The rock is considered too small to survive a plunge through Earth’s atmosphere and is not expected to approach closer than the Moon’s distance.
